en: *Collection of Names and Meanings of the Dharma Gates*, compiled by Li Shizheng, Academician of the Eastern Palace, following the instructions of Duke Yangcheng.

Preface by Li Shizheng: As for the essence of the Dharma, it is profound and tranquil; its true nature is impartial. Names and forms are fundamentally non-existent, and thus words and speech [are likewise so].
Yet, through the power of wisdom that realizes equality,
one thoroughly understands that the conditions are of a different nature and that the person who conditions them is quiescent.
Thus, one achieves unimpeded eloquence.
If one were to seal one's mouth and cease speaking,
how could the Sages transmit their transformative teachings?
When the deluded mind abandons the teaching,
ordinary delusions have no way to give rise to understanding;
therefore, the absence of speech does not hinder the joy of eloquent exposition.
By knowing that names do not exist, one does not destroy conventional designations;
through names, one penetrates quiescence.
Thus, the designation of dharmas serves as the gateway and path for explaining the meaning of names.
Should one not strive for this?
It is merely that it is distributed throughout various scriptures,
making it difficult to investigate exhaustively.
If one collects [these views] and explains them,
the *Yijing* becomes easy to observe.
Now, based on what has been seen...
Those details that remain unexplained are categorized by their commonalities,
forming a total of seven sections.
First is the body and mind;
second, faults and afflictions;
third, merits and virtues.
Section Four: Principle and Teaching;
Section Five: Worthies and Sages;
Section Six: Cause and Effect.
This is the seventh fruit of the world.
However, while the Dharma-gates are immeasurable,
my humble intellect has its limits.
It is like peering at the heavens through a tube,
or scooping up the ocean with a ladle;
one obtains the shallow while leaving behind the deep.
A thousand do not know one.
I request that those who have attained mastery provide the necessary supplements.
This is a brief summary of the names, enumerations, and classifications of the various dharma-gates.

Chapter One: The Dharma-Gate of the Meaning of Body and Mind. Regarding the meaning of the Dharma-gate of body and mind: First, the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—which combine in harmony to form the body.
Earth refers to the flesh, bones, and physical form;
water refers to the blood, marrow, and moisture;
fire refers to warmth.
Wind refers to the inhalation and exhalation of breath.
The six elements (mahābhūta) are earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
The four great elements were explained previously.
This "emptiness" (*ākāśa*) is the element of vast openness; "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is the mind of great discernment.
The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these five aggregates together constitute sentient beings.
Why is it called the aggregate of form?
Because physical obstruction constitutes form,
and experiencing constitutes sensation.
Conceptualization is termed "perception" (saṃjñā);
the arising and formation [of mental states] is termed "volitional formations" (saṃskāra);
and discernment is termed "consciousness" (vijñāna).
What is meant by "aggregates" (skandha)?
The aggregates are a collection that constitutes a sentient being.
The six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
These constitute the six sense faculties.
They give rise to the six consciousnesses as intermediate conditions.
Defilement is the consciousness’s engagement with the six sense objects.
Which object does the eye perceive?
It is form that disturbs its perception.
What object does the ear grasp?
Sound agitates the will.
What object does the nose defile?
Fragrances perfume their desires;
the tongue receives what objects?
Flavors increase their cravings.
What object does the body grasp?
It clings to the smooth and slippery.
What object does the mind become defiled by?
They flow into conceptual discrimination.
Why are they called "dust" (*rajas*)?

Because they are the objects of the six sense faculties; when combined with them, they give rise to defiled attachment that soils the mind and its intelligence, like the dust and grime that covers objects.
The six consciousnesses follow after sensory objects and obstruct the wisdom that is free from objects.
When the practitioner contemplates emptiness,
they attain the realization that is free from objects.
Therefore, one is able to remain unstained by sounds and forms,
not covet the flavors of the tongue,
and not be attached to tactile sensations.
Without giving rise to conceptual discrimination,
one penetrates the principle of non-conceptualization and attains the name of a sage.
Regarding the nine consciousnesses: those from the eye up to the mind constitute six, as has already been fully explained.
The seventh is the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness).
The eighth is the ālayavijñāna;
the ninth is the amala-vijñāna.
Including the preceding ones, these constitute nine.
What is meant by the term *ādāna*?
This is a word from the Western Regions (Sanskrit);
to speak according to its meaning:
The consciousness of the view of self:
the view of self in ordinary beings arises based on this consciousness,
obstructing the wisdom of non-self and preventing it from arising.
Only when a sage cultivates the meditative concentration that extinguishes the mind can they eliminate these delusions; specifically,
they eliminate the delusion of a self.
One attains the wisdom of non-self.
"Ālaya-vijñāna" is also a term from the Western Regions (Sanskrit).
Speaking in terms of its function,
it has two capacities:
first, it sustains the material sense faculties.
First, it causes them not to be destroyed;
second, it maintains the pure seeds so that they do not perish.
"Amala" is a term from the Western Regions; translated into this language,
it is called "pure consciousness" (viśuddha-vijñāna).
It is also called Buddha-nature and is likewise termed the Dharma-body;
its essence cultivates all virtues.
Originally pure,
it does not increase when abiding in the body of a sage,
nor does it decrease when dwelling in the body of an ordinary person.
There is only the distinction between being hidden or manifest,
but no difference of superior or inferior.
When obscured by afflictions, it is hidden.
It manifests only when realized through wisdom;
it is not produced by a productive cause,
but is attained through a revealing cause.
The twelve bases (āyatana): the eye base,
the ear base,
and the nose base.
The tongue sense-base,
the body sense-base,
and the mind sense-base.
The sense-base of visible forms,
the sense-base of sounds,
and the sense-base of odors.
The sense-base of taste,
the sense-base of tangibles,
and the sense-base of mental phenomena.
The six faculties, such as the eye,
constitute the six internal bases; the six objects, such as form, [constitute the six external bases].
In contrast to the channels through which consciousness arises,
these are the six external sense bases; thus,
there are two sets of six, internal and external.
These are the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
What is meant by "base"?
It refers to the channel through which consciousness arises from the mutual encounter of the sense faculties and their objects.
Because they receive and enter into love and hatred,
they are called "entrances" (āyatana).
The eighteen elements (dhātu) consist of the six faculties, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses.
Taken together, these three sets of six constitute the eighteen *dhātus*.
Why are they called *dhātus*? "Element" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of distinct nature (*prakṛti-viśeṣa*).
2. Chapter on Faults (Doṣa-varga): The Meaning of the Names of the Dharma-Gates. Chapter Two. The Two Extremes: The view of existence and the view of non-existence constitute the two extremes.
Furthermore, there are two extremes:
the view of annihilationism and the view of eternalism.
As for the view of existence:
Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is empty,
it cannot be grasped as existing.
This refers to those with the view of eternalism.
Although cause and effect perish,
karmic retribution is not lost;
it cannot be severed.
Those who hold the view of permanence [assert that] all phenomena are permanent; thus,
phenomena lack the characteristic of emptiness.
It cannot be regarded as permanent.
Why is it called an "extreme"?
Both emptiness and existence, as well as annihilationism and eternalism, are all heterodox and deviant.
Because it does not accord with the Middle Way,
it is called an "extreme" (anta).
As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
Although they practice in emptiness,
they plant the roots of all virtues;
although they practice in signlessness, they...
Yet they deliver all sentient beings;
though their practice is without arising,
they give rise to all wholesome deeds.
This is the practice of the bodhisattva’s detachment from extremes and non-attachment.
The three poisons are: greed, anger, and delusion.
This is ignorance (*moha*).
This poison can give rise to ten thousand faults.
The five desires: the desire for form (*rūpa-kāma*).
Desire for sounds,
desire for fragrances,
and desire for tastes.
The desire for touch—
these constitute the five desires.
Humans and devas receive the bliss of the five desires as the karmic reward of their merit.
Those who cultivate the Way relinquish them and do not cling to them.
Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"Although one should possess merit as its natural consequence..."
One should not indulge in self-indulgence;
one should contemplate the impermanence of the five desires in order to seek the root of goodness.
Regarding body, life, and wealth,
one should cultivate the firm Dharma.
The six thieves— the six consciousnesses— become defiled by sensory objects and give rise to the three poisons.
Because it destroys and harms meritorious virtues,
it is compared to a thief.
As the Sūtra says:
Furthermore, this thief of consciousness is that which wanders like a monkey among the six sense faculties.
Regarding the eight inversions: only the Great Nirvāṇa possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity, yet sentient beings perceive it as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure.
To perceive existence within non-existence— claiming that there is an infinite principle and a reality—
is therefore called "perversion. This refers to the two sets of four [errors] concerning the past and the future.
These are called the eight inversions.
The four inversions are: the inversion of permanence and the inversion of self.
The inversion of purity, the inversion of pleasure, and the inversion of self:
[one] regards all phenomena as permanent, pleasurable, and pure when they are actually impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Yet sentient beings perceive permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Furthermore, there are the four inversions and the five hindrances: the hindrance of sensual desire.
The hindrance of ill will,
the hindrance of sloth and torpor,
and the hindrance of restlessness and remorse.
The hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*). Why is it called a hindrance?
Because it is able to shroud the practitioner.
This is called a "hindrance" (āvaraṇa).
It covers and obscures the mind,
causing it to lack clarity.
These are called the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*):
the four afflictions, namely, the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and self-love (*ātmasneha*).
Ego-conceit and ignorance—
these are called the four afflictions.
This is the arising of the seventh ādāna-vijñāna.
The eight wrongs: wrong view, wrong intention, [wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration].
Wrong speech,
wrong action,
and wrong livelihood.
Wrong diligence,
wrong mindfulness,
and wrong concentration.
The nine grounds for resentment: hating my virtuous friends;
loving my enemies;
and hating my own person.
These three types of disagreeable [objects] each have three time periods.
This is what it means.
The three obstacles: the obstacle of afflictions,
the obstacle of karma,
and the obstacle of retribution.
The four māras: the māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*) is the cause of birth and death;
the māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*) and the māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*)—these two are the fruits of birth and death.
The celestial Māra and the Māra of birth-and-death are able to bring liberation through these four types;
therefore, they are called "Māras.
The ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*): first, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*).
2. Lack of shame;
3. Drowsiness;
4. Remorse.
5. Stinginess (mātsarya).
6. Envy (īrṣyā).
7. Resentment (pradāśa).
8. Sloth; 9. Anger;
10. Concealment.
The three outflows: the outflow of sensual desire,
the outflow of existence,
and the outflow of ignorance.
The sixty-two views: regarding the five aggregates of the past, each is reckoned perversely according to four propositions.
These four propositions concerning the past are as follows:
First, going as it truly is;
second, not going as it truly is;
third, both going as it truly is and not going as it truly is.
Fourth, neither going nor not going.
Regarding the five aggregates of the future, one calculates four propositions:
first, that they have an end.
Second, it is infinite;
third, it is both finite and infinite;
fourth, it is neither finite nor infinite.
Regarding each of the present aggregates (skandhas),
four propositions are posited:
first, permanence.
Second, impermanence;
third, both permanence and impermanence;
fourth, neither permanence nor impermanence.
For each of the two aggregates, four views arise;
these five aggregates combined total twenty views.
Calculated across the three time periods, they amount to sixty views in total.
In summary, the views of annihilationism and eternalism are taken as the root;
these constitute the sixty-two views.
Among the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the first is the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Second is the view of extremes.

Third is the grasping at views, which is the arising of attachment to tainted views. Fourth is the grasping at precepts and observances, which is the adherence to tainted precepts in pursuit of a pure fruit. Fifth is false view.
Sixth is greed;
seventh is anger;
eighth is delusion.
Ninth is pride;
tenth is doubt.
These five types, beginning with false view, are called the five sharp fetters (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*).
The five types of dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*), beginning with greed and hatred, are the [five] underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The five types of sharp afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*) constitute the afflictions of the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-kleśa*);
they are able to delude one regarding the true principle, preventing it from being seen.
The five types of dull afflictions constitute the defilements of the path of cultivation;
they are able to obstruct the practice cultivated within specific matters.
The person who has attained the stage of Srotāpanna has completely severed all afflictions pertaining to the truths of vision.
The Sakṛdāgāmin and Anāgāmin have not yet exhausted the afflictions of the path of cultivation;
the Arhat has exhausted the afflictions of both the wheel of seeing the truths and the path of cultivation within the three realms.
Therefore, one is not born within the three realms.
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna,
this messenger is employed to discern the afflictions (*kleśa*).
In the Mahāyāna teachings, the afflictions are distinguished by means of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*). These are: the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling;

the afflictions of the stage of dwelling in all places, which pervade the three realms; the afflictions of the stage of dwelling in desire-attachment, which are the afflictions of the desire realm; the afflictions of the stage of dwelling in form-attachment, which are the afflictions of the formless realm; and the [afflictions] of the three fruits and four stages of the Lesser Vehicle.
Because they have gradually severed the afflictions of the first four stages of dwelling (bhūmi) but have not yet exhausted them,
they undergo birth-and-death with limited segments within the triple world— namely,
Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas prior to the ten stages of worthiness.
Up to and including those at the tenth stage,
they have severed the afflictions of the four stages of abiding;
therefore, they escape the birth-and-death of segmented duration within the three realms.
There still remains the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), which is being gradually severed but not yet exhausted;
therefore, one undergoes the transformative birth-and-death (*nirmāṇa-cyuty-upapatti*) outside the three realms.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
The three kinds of mind-made bodies (manomayakāya) of Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of great power all undergo transformation.
As for these three kinds of mind-made bodies: they correspond to the first, second, and third stages (bhūmi).
The name *mābhūti* refers to the body born of the will (*manomaya-kāya*) of blissful intent.
On the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages,
it is called the body born of the will that realizes the self-nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*).
The seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages are called the "spontaneously born body produced by mental attention without effort" (*anābhoga-manasikāra-ja-nikāya-sahaja-kāya*).
Chapter Three: The Exposition on the Meaning of the Qualities of the Dharma-Gate. The Three Refuges: Taking refuge in the Buddha.
I take refuge in the Dharma.
I take refuge in the Saṅgha.
The Four Reliances: rely on the Dharma, not on the person.
Rely on the meaning, not on the words;
rely on wisdom, not on consciousness;
rely on sūtras of definitive meaning, not on sūtras of provisional meaning.
The Five Precepts: 1. Not to kill living beings;
2. Not to steal;
3. Not to engage in sexual misconduct.
Fourth, refraining from false speech.
Fifth, refraining from drinking intoxicants.
These constitute the five precepts.
The Jingdu jing (Sutra on Pure Deliverance) states:
"For those who maintain meditative concentration, Heaven ordains that five deities shall protect them.
For those who maintain the five precepts and meditative concentration, twenty-five deities shall guard their gates and doors, preventing evil from entering."
The Eight Precepts: First, not to kill;
second, not to steal;
third, not to engage in sexual misconduct.
Fourth, not to engage in false speech.
Fifth, not to drink alcohol.
Sixth, not to wear necklaces or ornaments.
Anointing the body with fragrant oils and perfuming one's garments with incense; seventh,
one must not engage in singing, dancing, or chanting, nor intentionally go to watch or listen to them.
Eighth, one must not lie upon a high, large, or wide bed.
These are the eight precepts;
these are the monastic precepts that a layperson observes for one day and one night.
The Ten Inexhaustible Precepts: First, not killing;
second, not stealing;
third, not engaging in sexual misconduct.
Fourth, not to engage in false speech.
Fifth, not to sell intoxicants.
Sixth, not to speak of the faults of monastic or lay bodhisattvas.
Seventh, not praising oneself or disparaging others out of greed for gain;
eighth, not being intentionally stingy;
ninth, not being intentionally angry.
Tenth, one must not intentionally slander the Triple Gem or its treasury.
From this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, one must not commit such an offense.
Should one commit such an offense, one shall suffer loss.
The forty-two dharmas of the noble ones constitute the bodhisattva precepts,
the threefold pure precepts (*tri-koṭi-viśuddha-śīla*). To cease all evil without exception is the precept of restraining oneself (*saṃvara-śīla*).
To cultivate every single wholesome dharma without exception is the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgraha-kuśala-dharma-śīla*).
To deliver every single sentient being without exception—
This is the precept of gathering in sentient beings.
These three clusters of precepts constitute the path of the bodhisattva.
The first is non-killing.
Second, not stealing;
third, not engaging in sexual misconduct;
fourth, not speaking falsehoods.
Fifth, no frivolous speech;
sixth, no double-tongued speech;
seventh, no harsh speech.
Eighth, freedom from covetousness.
Ninth, freedom from ill will.
Tenth, freedom from wrong views.
In the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are five kinds of the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*).
First, the ten wholesome actions of humans and devas;
second, the ten wholesome actions of śrāvakas.
Third, the ten wholesome actions of the pratyekabuddhas;
fourth, the ten wholesome actions of the bodhisattvas;
fifth, the ten wholesome actions of the Buddhas.
The distinctions among these five types are numerous and their meanings are extensive;
they are fully contained within the treatise and are not recorded here in detail.
The Six Recollections: First, the recollection of the Buddha.
The Buddha is the unsurpassed compassionate father of all sentient beings.
Second, the recollection of the Dharma.
The Dharma is the excellent medicine for the afflictions of sentient beings.
Third, one should mindfully recollect the Sangha;
the Sangha is the field of merit for the three vehicles of sentient beings.
The fourth is the mindfulness of precepts;
the precepts are that by which sentient beings guard against what is improper and cease from evil.
The fifth is the mindfulness of relinquishment.
Abandoning these sentient beings' stinginess and various attachments is the sixth recollection:
that of the devas. The devas are sentient beings who possess the pure karmic fruition.
This "heaven" is not the heaven of the triple world;
it refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Because it is pure, it is called "heaven."
The six points of harmonious respect: sameness of body,
sameness of speech,
and sameness of mind.
They are identical in their precepts,
identical in their giving,
and identical in their views.
These are called the six similarities.
They practice the Buddha-dharma equally,
remaining free from all pride and contention.
Therefore, it is called harmony and respect;
it is also called the straightforward mind.
The six perfections: the perfection of giving.
The perfection of ethical discipline,
the perfection of patience,
and the perfection of diligence.
The perfection of meditative concentration and the perfection of wisdom;
reaching the other shore is called "perfection" (pāramitā).
In the correct phonology of the Western Land, it is called *pāramitā*.
*Pāra* means "the other shore," and *mitā* means "to reach."
One has reached the other shore.
If one does not realize the emptiness of these three matters,
then even though one practices the six kinds of goodness, [it will not lead to liberation].
It is merely called "giving" and merely called "precept-keeping," but it cannot be termed a pāramitā.
The ten pāramitās consist of the six— generosity (dāna), ethical discipline (śīla), patience (kṣānti), vigor (vīrya), meditation (dhyāna), and wisdom (prajñā)—
with the addition of the seventh, the pāramitā of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā), which dedicates virtuous deeds and material gifts toward the attainment of results for others.
The first is called "superior wisdom of skillful means.

The eighth, which involves making vows and undertaking practice, is called "vow. The ninth, which subdues through power, observes the precepts, and eliminates hindrances, is called "power. The tenth, the wisdom that can know the dharma-gates of the six perfections, is called "wisdom."
This is called wisdom.
The four means of integration: the integration of giving, the integration of kind speech, [the integration of beneficial conduct, and the integration of common purpose].
The gathering through benefit and the gathering through common purpose;
by means of these four methods, the bodhisattva gathers and transforms sentient beings.
Therefore, they are called the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).

The four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇacitta*) are: immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī*), immeasurable compassion (*karuṇā*), [immeasurable sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and immeasurable equanimity (*upekṣā*)].
The immeasurable joy and the immeasurable equanimity;
loving-kindness is able to bestow happiness and provide benefit.
It is called "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*).
Because its objects are not restricted,
it is termed "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).
To compassionately rescue others from suffering and distress is called "compassion" (karuṇā);
to rejoice in their attainment is "joy" (muditā).
This is called joy (*muditā*).
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is able to eliminate both hatred and love,
so that the mind attains equality.
To be free from the three preceding states of mind and not to cling to signs is called equanimity.
The meaning of "immeasurable" is explained entirely as before.
The eight awakenings of a great person: having few desires and being content.
Tranquil purity,
diligence, and non-forgetfulness of mindfulness.
Right wisdom,
right concentration,
and non-proliferation.
The four practices of drawing near: drawing near to virtuous friends,
hearing the true Dharma,
and applying focused mindfulness through reflection.
Practicing in accordance with the Dharma,

one possesses the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*): the clear knowledge of past lives, the clear knowledge of the future through the divine eye, and [the clear knowledge of the destruction of the outflows].
Presently, there is the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*).
There are six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): first, the power of the body (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*);
second, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-jñāna*).
Third, the supernormal power of the divine ear;
fourth, the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others;
fifth, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives.
Sixth is the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).
Being free from obstruction and unimpeded,
it is called a "supernormal power" (*abhijñā*).
The eight liberations: First, possessing internal perception of form, one perceives external forms.
Initially, one contemplates impurity;
the path of contemplation is not yet strong.
One cannot destroy the internal body; rather,
by contemplating the external corpse as bloated,
one can eliminate the bonds of desire.
Therefore, it is called liberation.
Second, being internally without the perception of form, one perceives forms externally;
having practiced this for a long time.
As the contemplation of the path intensifies,
one is able to form the perception of the dissolution of the body and the extinction of form within oneself,
contemplating only the external corpse as bloated.
The third liberation of purity:
lovely colors such as blue, yellow, red,
and white are termed "pure."
Observing the pure and being free from fetters is called the liberation of purity;
this is the fourth liberation, the sphere of infinite space.
Seeking the formless is called emptiness; in the sphere of emptiness,
the four aggregates are free from bondage.
This is called the liberation of the sphere of infinite space.
The fifth is the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The objective sphere of space is vast and manifold.
When conditions are manifold, there is proliferation;
when the mind dwells upon objects with aversion,
it is termed consciousness (vijñāna).
The four aggregates in the sphere of consciousness, being free from bondage,
are called the liberation of the sphere of consciousness.
The sixth is the liberation of the non-existent as existent.
Because consciousness is manifold,
it causes the momentum of the mind to become fragmented;
if both mind and objects are extinguished, [the mind becomes unified].
That which is called "non-existence in all places" is a state free from bondage;
it is called liberation.
The seventh liberation is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Because the mental objects and states are coarse, they no longer manifest;
therefore, non-Buddhists call this the "state of mindlessness."
In the nature of the Buddha-dharma, there still remains subtle deliberation;
because it is described by combining the internal and external, it is called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The eighth is the liberation of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
When both the mind and mental factors cease together,
it is called the liberation of the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti-vimokṣa*).
By extinguishing all mental factors, one is freed from the fault of having a mind.
Therefore, it is called "liberation.
This is termed the eight liberations (aṣṭa-vimokṣa) and is also termed the eight relinquishments (aṣṭa-vaiśāradya).
To attain what is superior and abandon what is inferior is called "reversal" (prātikūlya);
these are the eight liberations (aṣṭa-vimokṣa).
The three types of wisdom: the wisdom of hearing,
the wisdom of reflection,
and the wisdom of cultivation.
The two knowledges: the knowledge of the true nature of reality (dharmatā-jñāna) and the knowledge of skillful means (upāya-jñāna).
Furthermore, there are two other knowledges.
The wisdom of suchness,
the wisdom of suchness-in-measure,
the four wisdoms, and the knowledge that "birth has been exhausted."
The knowledge that the holy life has been established;
the knowledge that what was to be done has been accomplished;
and the knowledge that there will be no further existence.
There are two paths: first, the path of seeing (darśana-mārga);
second, the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga).
As for the path of seeing:
To clearly comprehend the names is called "seeing" (*darśana*);
to further illuminate them is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
Seeing is understanding.
"Cultivating the path" means practicing this cultivation;
it is able to remove obstructions.
This is called the Path.
There are four types of cultivation: uninterrupted cultivation and long-term cultivation.
Practicing with reverence,
practicing without remainder,
and practicing without interruption.
Because evil and neutral states cannot intervene,
it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*).
As for "cultivating over a long period":
The three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas are of such immense duration;
yet those who practice with reverence [attain it].
Revering people and honoring the Dharma,
one should exhaust oneself in the utmost sincerity;
there is no other practice to be cultivated.
Cultivate great compassion and the practice of benefiting others for all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma realm.
Cultivating sublime wisdom,
he perfected the practice of self-benefit and attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Being fully complete and satisfying,
with nothing left unattended,
it is therefore called "cultivation without remainder."
The ten knowledges: first, the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna);
second, subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna);
third, the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna).
Fourth, the knowledge of others' minds;
fifth, the knowledge of suffering;
sixth, the knowledge of origination.
7. Knowledge of cessation;
8. Knowledge of the path;
9. Knowledge of exhaustion.
The ten knowledges of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) and the five patiences (*kṣānti*): first, the patience of submissiveness (*adhimukti-kṣānti*);
second, the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*).
Third, the patience of conformity;
fourth, the patience of non-arising;
fifth, the patience of cessation.
Bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness prior to the grounds attain the patience of subduing (kṣānti-vinaya).
Those of the first, second, and third grounds attain the patience of faith (śraddhā-kṣānti).
Those of the fourth, fifth, and sixth grounds attain the patience of conformity (anuloma-kṣānti).
In the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
In the tenth stage and the Buddha-stage, one attains the patience of cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*).
The ten perceptions (*daśa-saṃjñā*) are: the perception of impermanence (*anitya-saṃjñā*).
The perception of suffering;
the perception of emptiness and non-self;
and the perception of repulsiveness in food.
The perception of the lack of delight in all worlds,
the perception of death,
and the perception of impurity.
The perception of abandonment,
the perception of dispassion,
and the perception of cessation.
The four dhyānas: the dhyāna practiced by foolish worldlings;
the dhyāna of contemplating the perception of meaning;
and the dhyāna of focusing on true suchness (*tathatā*).
The dhyāna of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas consists of the twelve dhūtas: first, begging for food for as long as one lives;
second, dwelling in an araṇya.
Third, wearing rag-robes;
fourth, eating in a single sitting;
fifth, always remaining seated.
Sixth, one does not accept food outside of the proper time after midday.
Seventh, one does not drink liquids after midday.
Eighth, one possesses only the three robes.
Ninth, wearing garments of wool;
tenth, sitting at the foot of a tree;
eleventh, dwelling in an open space.
Twelfth is dwelling among corpses.
The ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*)— earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, space, and consciousness—
are these universal bases.
The eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*): first, having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as limited;
second, having the perception of internal forms...
Third, having no perception of internal forms,
one perceives external forms as few.
Fourth, one has no perception of internal forms and perceives external forms as manifold.
Fifth, one has no perception of internal forms.
Sixth, internally perceiving no form,
one externally perceives forms that are predominantly yellow.
Seventh, being internally percipient of no form,
one perceives externally a small amount of red color.
Eighth, being internally percipient of no form...
Externally, it appears predominantly white.
It consists of the fivefold Dharma-body: the body of precepts (śīla-kāya) and the body of meditative concentration (samādhi-kāya).
The body of wisdom,
the body of liberation,
and the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
These are called the five dharmas of the body.
Precept (*śīla*) means guarding against what is improper and ceasing evil.
Concentration (*samādhi*) means the mind abiding in a single object.
The wise person makes a definitive resolution regarding the objects of perception;
one whose body is liberated severs all bonds and casts off all fetters.
Regarding the body of knowledge and vision of liberation:
within the conditions for liberation,
one examines them until they are clear and evident.
Because this fivefold dharma-body is the essential nature of the Buddha’s virtues,
it is called the "body" for the sake of exposition.
The seven purifications: purification of virtue,
purification of concentration,
and purification of view.
Purity through transcendence;
purity through the path and non-path;
purity through the cessation of formations.
The supreme dharmas conducive to enlightenment and the purification of the supreme [path].
The seven riches: faith, ethical discipline, generosity, learning, wisdom, shame, and dread of blame—these are called the seven riches.
It is called "wealth" because it can support and assist the true path.
It has four characteristics: being correct oneself and correcting others.
He is able to respond appropriately to questions and is well-versed in the meaning of causes and conditions.
The four minds: the vast mind.
The foremost mind,
the constant mind,
the non-perverted mind.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment: the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts,
and the four bases of power.
The five faculties,
the five powers,
and the seven factors of enlightenment.
The Eightfold Noble Path.
Taken together, these are enumerated as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), there are differences in their nomenclature between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Contemplate the impurity of the body;
contemplate the suffering inherent in sensation;
contemplate the arising and ceasing of the mind.
Contemplating the selflessness of phenomena is the four foundations of mindfulness of the Hīnayāna;
contemplating the body as being like empty space.
Contemplate that feelings are empty internally and externally;
contemplate that the mind is merely a name;
and contemplate that dharmas, whether wholesome or unwholesome, are both unobtainable.
This is the Mahāyāna four foundations of mindfulness and the four right efforts:
the skillful means to prevent unwholesome states that have not yet arisen from arising.
The first right effort is to employ skillful means to eliminate unwholesome states that have already arisen. The second right effort is... [to prevent unwholesome states from arising].
The three right efforts consist of employing skillful means to cause wholesome states that have not yet arisen to arise,
and employing skillful means to cause wholesome states that have already arisen to increase.
The four right efforts (samyak-prahāṇa) and the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhi-pāda), namely,
the base of psychic power consisting of desire (chanda-ṛddhi-pāda).
The basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through mindfulness,
the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through diligence,
and the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through wisdom.
The five faculties: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, [the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom].
The faculty of mindfulness,
the faculty of concentration,
and the faculty of wisdom.
That which is able to produce what follows is called a faculty (*indriya*).
The five powers (*bala*).
The power of faith,
the power of diligence,
and the power of mindfulness.
The power of concentration and the power of wisdom;
the former can master the latter.
The power of mindfulness consists of the seven factors of enlightenment,
beginning with the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness.
The awakening factor of diligence,
the awakening factor of joy,
and the awakening factor of tranquility.
The factor of enlightenment of concentration, the factor of enlightenment of equanimity,
and the factor of enlightenment of discernment.
The Eightfold Noble Path:
Right View and Right Intention.
Right speech,
right action,
and right livelihood.
Right effort,
right mindfulness,
and right concentration.
The ten powers: the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible;
the power of karma;
the power of meditative concentration.
The power of the faculties,
the power of desire,
and the power of nature.
The power of the path leading to the destination,
the power of recollecting past lives,
and the power of the divine eye.
The power of the destruction of the outflows.
These are the ten powers of a Buddha.
The power of the possible and the impossible.
Virtue brings forth pleasant retribution;
evil yields bitter fruit.
Cause and effect correspond exactly.
That which is called "this possibility" (sthāna) is the opposite of the aforementioned;
that which is called "impossibility" (asthāna) is its contrary.
The Buddha knows both what is possible and what is impossible exactly as they truly are;
this is called the power of knowing the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).
Second is the power of karma:
the various karmas of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time,
and the places where those karmas were created.
He knows, exactly as it is, the places where retribution is experienced;
this is called the power of karma.
The third is the power of concentration,
which distinguishes between the defilement and purity within all meditative absorptions.
To know all things as they truly are is called the power of concentration. This is the fourth power,
the power of the faculties.
To know, as they truly are, the superior and inferior characteristics of the faculties of all sentient beings—
this is called the power of the faculties (indriyabala).
The power of the five desires.
To know the various desires of other sentient beings is called the power of desire.
Sixth is the power of nature (*dhātu-bala*).
To know the various natures of all worlds is called the power of nature.
Seventh is the power of the knowledge of the destinations of all paths.
To know the characteristics of the destinations reached by all paths is called the power of the knowledge of the destinations of all paths.
Eighth is the power of recollecting past lives.
To know the various past lives of all sentient beings is called the power of recollecting past lives.
Ninth is the power of the divine eye.
The Buddha’s divine eye is purer than that of humans and devas;
with it, he beholds all sentient beings.
There is nothing he does not see;
this is the power of the divine eye.
Tenth is the power of the exhaustion of outflows.
The Buddha knows, as it truly is, that all outflows are exhausted and liberation is attained;
this is called the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayabala*).
It refers to the afflictions, fetters, latent tendencies, defilements, and the continuous flow [of suffering].
This is called an outflow (*āsrava*).
The state where there are no outflows is called the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
By means of the Tathāgata’s wisdom,
these ten objects are illuminated to their ultimate limit.
Because they are without fault and without concealment, they are called powers (*bala*).
The four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*): the fearlessness of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-vaiśāradya*).
The fearlessness regarding the destruction of the outflows;
the fearlessness regarding the teaching on the obstacles to the path;
and the fearlessness regarding the teaching on the path leading to the end of suffering.
Regarding the fearlessness of omniscience,
the Buddha made this truthful declaration:
"I am one who possesses perfect and complete knowledge."
No human or deva is able to challenge this as it truly is by saying,
"This dharma is not known," nor do they perceive even the slightest sign of fear.
The fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows:
The Buddha makes this solemn declaration:
"I have exhausted all outflows."
No one is able to challenge him with words according to reality,
saying that his outflows are not yet exhausted,
nor can they perceive even the slightest sign of fear.
He speaks with fearlessness regarding the hindrances to the Path.
The Buddha makes this solemn declaration:
"I have taught the dharmas that constitute hindrances."
No one is able to challenge him with words according to reality,
nor can any obstructing dharma obstruct the Path;
indeed, he does not perceive even the slightest sign of fear.
The delusive dharmas that obstruct the noble ones are called "obstructions to the path.
He teaches the path to the exhaustion of suffering with fearlessness.
The Buddha spoke these truthful words:
"I declare that the Noble Path can transcend the world;
by practicing it accordingly, one can bring an end to suffering."
No one among gods or humans can rightfully challenge this by saying:
"Practicing this path of the noble ones does not transcend the world,
nor can it bring an end to suffering."
Even to the point of not perceiving the slightest sign of fear,
being able to eliminate the afflictions is called the exhaustion of suffering.
Fearlessness regarding difficulties is called "fearlessness.
The four types of unimpeded knowledge are: unimpeded knowledge of meaning, and unimpeded knowledge of phenomena.
The unimpeded knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*). The unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the reason for [the application of] names.
It is designated as "meaning" (artha).
Since "dharma" is the name for its own meaning,
it is designated as "dharma."
The speech that articulates the Dharma is called "eloquence" (pratibhāna). It is the joyful exposition that,
according to the desires [of others], skillfully imparts [the teaching].
It is called "eloquence" (pratibhāna);
because it is skillfully proficient and unimpeded,
it is termed "unobstructed wisdom" (pratisaṃvid).
The eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*): first, the Buddhas have no failure of body.
Their bodily conduct is virtuous and compliant;
this is called "no failure of body."
Second, there is no failure of speech.
When the karma of speech is virtuous and compliant,
it is called "no failure of speech."
Third is non-loss of mindfulness.
To have mindfulness that accords with reality without deviation is called non-loss of mindfulness.
Fourth is the absence of differential characteristics.
Protecting with equal moderation toward both enemies and kin is called the absence of differential thought.
Fifth, he has no unsettled mind;
he constantly abides in samādhi without a moment's distraction.
Therefore, it is called "having no unconcentrated mind.
Sixth, there is "no relinquishing without full knowledge.
Regarding matters such as the coarse and the subtle, nothing passes through the mind that is not first known before being discerned.
Therefore, it is said that once ignorance has been abandoned, there is no further need for knowledge.
Seventh is the non-diminution of aspiration;
one’s aspiration is perfectly fulfilled.
This is called "no decrease.
Eighth is the non-decrease of diligence;
one practices with tireless application.
This is called diligence.
Ninth is the non-diminution of mindfulness:
binding the mind to guard the object.
This is called mindfulness.
Tenth is the non-diminution of wisdom:
it is the decisive discernment regarding objects of cognition.
This is called wisdom.
Eleventh, liberation is undiminished;
he is severed from bonds and freed from fetters.
This is called liberation.
Twelfth is the non-diminution of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
one is able to clearly and intelligently illuminate and comprehend liberation.
This is called the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Because he knows that it is fulfilled, it is said to be without decrease.
Thirteenth, his bodily actions proceed in accordance with wisdom.
Physical form and movement are called bodily action (kāyakarma).
Because the body conforms to wisdom, it is said to "follow" (anuvartate).
Fifteenth, mental action proceeds in accordance with wisdom.
That which involves reflection upon what is to be done is called mental action.
Sixteenth, his wisdom knows the past without obstruction.
Because things have ceased and passed away, they are called "past.
He is able to know the objects of the past completely and universally.
Seventeenth: Wisdom knows the future world without obstruction.
That which is not yet manifest is called "the future."
Eighteenth, wisdom knows the future realm without obstruction;
events have arisen but have not yet passed away.
This is called the present.
To penetrate and fully know the objects of the present—
these eighteen kinds belong exclusively to the Buddha alone.
Because it does not extend to the lower fruits, it is called the "unshared dharma.
The ten titles [of the Buddha] are: Tathāgata.
Worthy of offerings,
perfectly and fully awakened,
perfect in knowledge and conduct.
Sugata, Knower of the World,
Unsurpassed One.
The Tamer of Men,
Teacher of Gods and Humans,
Buddha Bhagavān.
These are the ten titles.
Because the Tathāgata has come by means of the path of reality and attained perfect enlightenment, he is called the Tathāgata.
Because he is worthy of offerings and internally possesses wisdom and the abandonment [of defilements], receiving the offerings of devas and humans, he is called the Arhat.
Therefore, he is named the Worthy One (Arhat),
the Perfectly Enlightened One (Samyaksaṃbuddha),
who has understood and abandoned all error and delusion.
To name this "Correct," it reflects all objects;
thus it is called "Perfectly Complete Enlightenment" (Samyak-saṃbodhi).
Regarding the "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (Vidyācaraṇasampanna):
because his knowledge and conduct are without deficiency, he is called "Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct.
Regarding the "Well-Gone One" (Sugata):
"Excellent! It is 'departing.
Departing means going to nirvana."
Because he will never return again, it is said that he has "gone well.
As for "knower of the world," this refers to both sentient beings and the physical vessel-world.
There are two kinds of worlds;
because his wisdom illuminates them with clarity,
he is called the Knower of the Worlds.
The Unsurpassed One is one whose merit and wisdom are fully perfected,
surpassing all other beings.
Because there is no one who can equal him,
he is named the Unsurpassed One (Anuttarapuruṣa).
As for "the Tamer of Men" (Puruṣadamyasārathi):
By means of the supreme dharmas of the three vehicles,
he disciplines and adjusts beings according to their individual capacities;
therefore, he is called the "Tamer of Men" (Puruṣadamyasārathi).
The Teacher of Gods and Humans:
because his virtue is complete and he provides instruction and guidance to both gods and humans,
he is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
In this context, "Buddha" is translated as "Awakened" (jue).
Because his awakening is unimpeded, he is called a Buddha.
As for "Bhagavān":
He is called Bhagavat because he has destroyed the afflictions.
The five eyes are: the flesh eye, the divine eye, [the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the buddha eye].
The eye of wisdom,
the Dharma-eye,
and the Buddha-eye.
These are the five eyes.
The fleshly eye perceives forms that are obstructed and near;
the divine eye perceives forms that are unobstructed and distant.
The wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus) illuminates and contemplates emptiness;
the dharma-eye (dharma-cakṣus) illuminates existence;
the buddha-eye (buddha-cakṣus) illuminates both emptiness and existence simultaneously.
It clearly surpasses the four eyes;
that which they cannot know is here entirely clear and pure.
Generally speaking,
the term "eye" is established because its functions vary according to the differences among their respective objects;
for this reason, it is divided into five types.
The thirty-two marks of a great man: first, the soles of the feet are level and firm;
second, there are thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of the feet;
third, the fingers are slender and long.
Fourth, his heels are broad and prominent.
Fifth, his hands and feet are webbed.
Sixth, his hands and feet are soft and supple.
Seventh, his calves are like those of the eneya deer king.
Eighth, his ankle bones are not visible.
Ninth, when standing upright with his body straight, his hands reach down to touch his knees.
Tenth, his private parts are concealed within a sheath like those of a horse king.
Eleventh, his body is perfectly rounded like the nyagrodha tree.
Twelfth, the hairs on his body point upward.
Thirteenth, each hair curls to the right.
Fourteenth, his body is the color of gold.
Fifteenth, he has a halo extending one fathom.
Sixteenth, his skin is fine and soft, such that dust and grime do not adhere to it.
Seventeenth, the two hands, the two feet, the two shoulders, and the crown of the head—these seven places are full and well-rounded.
Eighteenth, his torso is like that of a lion king.
Nineteenth, his arms and elbows are rounded and well-proportioned.
Twentieth, the bones of his shoulders are level and full.
Twenty-first, his body is straight and well-proportioned.
Twenty-second: forty teeth. Twenty-third:
teeth that are white and pure.
Twenty-fourth: teeth that are even and closely set.
Twenty-fifth, the jawbones are square like those of a lion.
Twenty-sixth, among successive flavors, he obtains the supreme flavor.
Twenty-seventh, the mark of the fleshly protuberance on the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*).
Twenty-eighth, his tongue is broad and long;
twenty-ninth, his voice is like that of Brahmā;
thirtieth, his eyes are the color of deep blue.
Thirty-first: his upper and lower eyelids blink like those of a king.
Thirty-second: he has a white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
These are the eighty secondary marks (anuvyañjana). Below the throat are sixty kinds of secondary marks.
The twenty secondary marks above the throat constitute the eighty secondary marks;
those below the throat number sixty.
The twenty toes and fingers are complete; the eight areas of the hands and feet—both the palms and soles—are flat and full.

The two ankles, two knees, two calves, two shoulders, two wrists, two thighs, two upper arms, the concealed organs, the two circles [of the navel], the two biceps, the two sides, the two armpits, the two breasts, the waist, the back, the heart, the navel, and the throat are all perfectly formed and exquisite.
These are called the six kinds of ten excellences below the throat and the twenty above the throat.
As for those above and below: the two ears, teeth, lips, gums, cheeks, hair of the head and beard, eyes, ears, nostrils, eyebrows, foreheads, and temples.
The above are called the twenty secondary marks (anuvyañjana) upon the throat.
If one violates the precepts, they will not even attain the body of a lowly person;
how much less could they possess the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa)?
Furthermore, there are three kinds of immeasurability regarding the excellence of the leaves.
Cultivating them for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* is called immeasurability of time.
Bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings is called immeasurability of mind.
Various kinds of wholesome karma are called the "immeasurable practices.
By praising their virtues and cultivating the necessary requisites, one brings forth the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) of a Tathāgata.
Chapter Four: The Dharma-Gate of the Meaning of Principle and Teaching. Regarding the three types of Buddha: the Dharma-Buddha.
The Reward Buddha and the Response Buddha—
these are the three Buddhas.
The Dharma-Buddha is the Dharma-body of the Buddha;
it is therefore called the Dharma-Buddha.
Both ordinary beings and sages possess [this nature];
they differ only in its concealment or manifestation.
As long as the obstacles of delusion have not been eliminated, [it remains hidden].
The nature of the Buddha is eternally hidden;
once afflictions are exhausted,
the Dharma-body then manifests.
It arises solely from the revealing cause;
it does not arise from the productive cause. It exists [thereby].
Regarding the "Reward Buddha" (Bhoga-buddha):
the reward body of the Buddha is called the Reward Buddha.
Cultivating causes and attaining results is called "retribution.
As for the "Responsive Buddha" (Nirmāṇakāya):
The response-body of the Buddha is called the Responsive Buddha;
it manifests in accordance with the afflictions.
This is termed "correspondence.
At the outset, one practices hearing, contemplation, and cultivation;
through these practices, one is able to contemplate and realize that the dharma-body gives rise to the reward and correspondence bodies.
Therefore, the *Prajñā-śāstra* states:
"Regarding reality, it serves as the cause for individual realization and also as the generative cause for other [phenomena]."
The Three Jewels: the Buddha Jewel,
the Dharma Jewel,
and the Sangha Jewel.
The Three Jewels are of three kinds.
The first is the Three Jewels of the Single Essence (*eka-rasa-triratna*).
Within the essence of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), there is wondrous enlightenment (*prajñā*).
That which is named the Buddha Jewel possesses the wondrous patterns within the body of the Dharma-nature;
this is named the Dharma Jewel.
The Dharma-body, being free from opposition and contention,
is called the Sangha Jewel.
Second are the Three Jewels of distinct characteristics.
The sixteen-foot transformation body is taken as the Buddha-jewel;
the teaching of the Dharma is not spoken of as the Dharma-jewel.
This applies to those from the stage of the ten faiths of the Mahayana upward.
Those from the first fruit of the Hīnayāna upward are called the Saṃgha Jewel.
Third is the Saṃgha Jewel as the sustainer of the Three Jewels.
Mudra niches and plain statues are taken as the Buddha-jewel;
paper, silk, bamboo, and cloth are taken as the Dharma-jewel;
and ordinary persons and bhikṣus are taken as the Saṃgha-jewel.

The Tripiṭaka consists of: the Sūtra Piṭaka, which elucidates the two trainings of ethical discipline (śīla) and meditative concentration (samādhi), and according to the capacities of beings, cures their afflictions;
and the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The Vinaya Piṭaka exclusively elucidates the training in ethical discipline;
the Mātṛkā Piṭaka exclusively elucidates the training in wisdom.
It is also called the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
These three piṭakas are divided into two collections according to the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles,
namely, the Śrāvaka Piṭaka and the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
The Three Vehicles: the Śrāvaka Vehicle,
the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle,
and the Buddha-Bodhisattva Vehicle.
The five vehicles: the vehicle of humans,
the vehicle of devas,
and the vehicle of śrāvakas.
The vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas and the vehicle of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to transport sentient beings from cause to fruition.
Therefore, it is called a "vehicle" (yāna).
Regarding the two truths: the first is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), also known as the worldly truth (loka-satya).
The second is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), also called the true truth (*bhūta-satya*).

This refers to the fact that phenomena as objects of cognition do not themselves possess names or functions; rather, their characteristics are manifested through ten thousand differentiated verbal expressions.
All these are conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
"Truth" (*satya*) means reality.
That which is real for ordinary beings is [conventional truth].
Because it is not real from the perspective of the noble ones,
it is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), reality and delusion are equal, and defilement and purity are non-dual.
Whatever is without substance, without characteristics,
and without verbal designation is entirely subsumed within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
It is only the supramundane noble ones (ārya) who realize this principle.
It is most real and peerless;
therefore, it is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
The Buddhas' teaching of the Dharma relies upon two truths;
together they express a single reality without mutual contradiction.
Therefore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"There is no self, no agent,
and no one who receives the karma of good and evil."
The former clarifies that there is no creator or recipient;
the latter explains the existence of good and evil.
How could the preceding and following statements be mutually contradictory?
Therefore, there is a principle and a coherent connection;
one must not adopt them in isolation.
There are people in the world who cling to emptiness while turning their backs on the teachings;
are they not utterly deluded?
The Four Noble Truths: the Truth of Suffering.
The truth of origination,
the truth of cessation,
and the truth of the path.
These are the Four Noble Truths.
There are two types of the Four Noble Truths:
first, the Four Noble Truths of conditioned activity belonging to the Hīnayāna.
Second is the Mahāyāna’s unconditioned Four Noble Truths:
birth-and-death as the fruit is suffering;
the afflictions are the truth of origination.
This quiescent extinction is called the noble truth of cessation.
Attaining the Path by means of non-dual dharmas is called the noble truth of the path.
In the Mahāyāna’s four noble truths of non-action,
one contemplates the noble truth of suffering and realizes that the origin of suffering is without conjunction.
"This is the noble truth of suffering.
"Knowing that there is no cessation where there is already cessation—
this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering."
One attains the Way through the dharma of non-duality;
this is called the Noble Truth of the Path.
The Three Dharma Seals: All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
All phenomena are without self;
nirvāṇa is quiescent extinction.
Impermanent, conditioned, and produced by causes, the substance of phenomena arises dependent upon conditions.
Because change and transformation are not constant, they are called "impermanent.
All phenomena (*dharma*) are without self; their essence lacks substantial reality or the power of sovereignty.
Therefore, it is called "selflessness.
Specifically, according to the Mahāyāna, regarding the two types of selflessness—person-selflessness and phenomenon-selflessness—and nirvāṇa as quiescence:
the three poisons and six impurities are forever abandoned without remainder.
The nature of the mountain is tranquil and serene;
this is called "nirvana" (寂滅).
According to the Mahayana, it also encompasses cessation through principle (理滅).
These three dharmas are all called "seals" (*mudrā*) because they are fixed and unshakable.
The six defilements (*kaṣāya*) are: malice, resentment, vexation, deceit, arrogance, and flattery.
The four *udāna*: All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
all conditioned phenomena are suffering;
all phenomena are non-self.
Nirvana is quiescent extinction.
There are four kinds of *siddhāntas*: the worldly *siddhānta*, the individual *siddhānta*, [the therapeutic *siddhānta*, and the ultimate *siddhānta*].
The therapeutic standpoint (pratipakṣa-siddhānta) and the ultimate standpoint (paramārtha-siddhānta):
these four standpoints encompass all twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Together with the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma,
all are entirely true and without contradiction.
Within the Buddha-dharma, there is that which is real by way of the world-standpoint (loka-siddhānta);
there is that which is real by way of the therapeutic-standpoint (pratipakṣa-siddhānta);
and there is that which is real by way of the ultimate-standpoint (paramārtha-siddhānta).
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Buddhadvirātra-sūtra*:
"From the night the Buddha attained the Way until the night of his parinirvāṇa—
whatever sūtras and teachings were spoken during the interval between these two nights [constitute the *dvirātra*]."
"All are real and not inverted.
This name for the *siddhānta*, along with its subsequent explanation,
is both extracted from the first fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The twelve divisions of the scriptures:
Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa.
Gāthā, Udāna, and Nidāna.
Avadāna, Itivṛttaka, and Jātaka.
Vaipulya, Avidūradharma, and Upadeśa.
It constitutes the treasury of names for the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
As for the *sūtra*,
it refers to all the fundamental sūtras and all the principles of the treatises.
From "Thus have I heard" up to "rejoiced and practiced accordingly," regardless of the number of fascicles,
all are called *sūtra*.
Geṇya refers to verses that state the truth without repetition.
Vyākaraṇa-sūtra refers to such as when Śākyamuni Tathāgata bestowed a prophecy upon Maitreya, saying:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha."
This is a *vyākaraṇa* (prediction).
A *geya* is a verse that is a restatement of prose rather than a direct exposition.
An *udāna* is a discourse spoken spontaneously without being questioned.
The *Nidāna* refers to the Sūtras on Causes and Conditions;
the *Avadāna* refers to the Sūtras of Parables;
and the *Itivṛttaka* refers to the Sūtras on Worldly Realms.
It is also called the *Itivṛttaka* (Scriptures of Past Occurrences).
The *Jātaka* (Birth Stories) refers to those accounts of the physical bodies the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, assumed when he was formerly a bodhisattva.
Vaipulya refers to the extensive sūtras; that is to say,
the Mahāyāna Vaipulya scriptures, the meaning of which is vast and expansive.
It is just like space.
"Abudhadharma" means that which has never before occurred.
Just as when the Buddha was first born, he took seven steps in each of the ten directions;
the monkey Māndhātṛ offered him a vessel of honey;
and the white-necked dog listened to the Dharma.
These and others such as these are the *Adbhutadharma* (Marvels) Sūtras.
The *Upadeśa* (Exegesis) Sūtras are those that discuss the meaning of the teachings.
For example, there are those sūtras spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, which provide detailed analysis and exposition on the characteristics and faculties of the orators.
The three kinds of prajñā: first, the prajñā of ultimate reality;
second, the prajñā of contemplative illumination;
and third, the prajñā of words and letters.
The prajñā of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā) takes principle as its essence.
Since its essence is utterly free from the false and provisional,
it is designated as "real."
The manifestation of the essence of the seal is termed its "mark" (lakṣaṇa); yet,
it may also be characterized by its very lack of marks.
The wisdom of contemplative observation (pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā) takes wisdom as its essence;
the essence is prajñā,
while contemplative observation is its function.
Because it explains both essence and function together, it is called "contemplative prajñā.
Textual prajñā takes the elucidation through vocal teachings as its essence;
the text itself is not prajñā.
Why is it called *prajñā*?
First, because it can give rise to *prajñā*;
second, because it can express *prajñā*.
Prajñā is established because the fruit is spoken of within the cause.
There are two kinds of nirvāṇa: first, nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity;
second, nirvāṇa through skillful means.
The principle of innate purity and natural truth pervades the three periods of time;
its virtues are perfectly complete.
Fundamentally, there is neither increase nor decrease;
though it appears or disappears according to conditions,
its essence remains free from defilement and entanglement.
Therefore, in accordance with reality, its name is revealed:
it is called "Nirvana of Innate Purity" (prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa). [Next is] "Nirvana of Purification through Expedient Means" (upāya-viśuddhi).
Sentient beings, having received their consciousness,
though they possess true nature,
are shrouded by afflictions and delusions such that their minds cannot turn back toward themselves.
One must rely upon the guidance and instruction of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra);
only then can one accord with the teachings, transmit the cultivation of insight into phenomena,
and gradually increase one's understanding and contemplation.
When afflictions and delusions are completely cast off, the body, its functions, and conduct are perfected; this is the fruition of the application of skillful means.
Thus, the fruit is not self-inflicted, but is accomplished through the subtle and precise mastery of function that extinguishes all burdens.
Therefore, that which is capable of acting as its own designation is called "purification through skillful means" (*upāya-viśuddhi*).

Within this, the five sense organs and six objects of the discriminative nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) constitute the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); the essence of consciousness of the discriminative nature constitutes the dependent nature; and true suchness (*tathatā*) of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) constitutes the perfected nature.
There are two kinds of selflessness: first, the selflessness of persons;
second, the selflessness of phenomena.
The selflessness of persons is also called the emptiness of sentient beings.
This is also called the emptiness of persons.
From the emptiness of sentient beings up to the emptiness of the Buddha—
this is called the emptiness of persons.
It is refuted by the analogy of "tortoise hair.
The absence of self in phenomena is also called the emptiness of phenomena;
the five aggregates of sentient beings are empty.
Even unto the five aggregates of the Buddha being empty—
this is the emptiness of dharmas.
The five aggregates are the dharmas that constitute a sentient being.
The five aggregates are empty in essence;
this is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
The above refutes the [existence of] a rabbit's horn.
The three natures of non-existence: first, the nature of signlessness;
second, the nature of arising through designation;
third, the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature.
Regarding the nature of signlessness (*animitta-lakṣaṇatā*):
phenomena such as the sense faculties and their objects are fundamentally quiescent according to the principle;
this is called the nature of signlessness.
Regarding the nature of non-arising:
according to principle, the fundamental consciousness and other mental states do not arise;
this is termed the nature of non-arising.
Regarding the nature of non-nature:
when both of the preceding two [natures] are simultaneously extinguished, it is called the nature of non-nature;
the essence of this non-nature is one.
Because they follow from the means of expression, three names are established for them.
The true dharma is free from characteristics;
it is called the "nature of the absence of nature."
The three emptinesses: first, the samādhi of emptiness;
second, the samādhi of signlessness;
third, the samādhi of wishlessness.
The designation of the "three emptinesses" arises from deluded conceptualization.
Although such deluded conceptualizations are numerous,
their general synthesis consists of only three.
Regarding the delusions, one distinguishes emptiness;
emptiness is likewise threefold.
As for the three delusions:
First, because there is stagnation in existence, it is dispelled by emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Second, because there are characteristics of existence, they are removed by signlessness (*animitta*).
Third, because there is the persistence of emotional aspiration, it is washed away by wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
The aggregates arising from the emptiness-samādhi are devoid of reality;
both are taken as empty.
Defilements cease within this emptiness.
It is called the samādhi of emptiness.
The samādhi of signlessness is so named because it is empty and devoid of all characteristics, thereby being signless.
To concentrate the mind on signlessness is called the samādhi of signlessness.
The samādhi of wishlessness is the rarefied seeking of the meaning of emptiness.
To regard [all things] as wishless (*apraṇihita*).
To be at ease and free from wishes is called the *Apraṇihita-samādhi*. Its original Sanskrit term is *Samādhi*; in the Han language, it means "harmonious and direct."
The three unconditioned phenomena: the unconditioned phenomenon of analytical cessation,
the unconditioned phenomenon of non-analytical cessation,
and the unconditioned phenomenon of space.
The unconditioned state of cessation through analytical knowledge is common to both the Great and Small Vehicles;
they employ the categories of the wisdom aggregate to sever the afflictions.

That which is extinguished through analytical discernment is called the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation; that which is not [extinguished] through analytical discernment is the unconditioned state of cessation not through deliberation.
That is to say, all things in the world that come into being must inevitably perish;
after a long time, they extinguish themselves of their own accord,
not through the deliberate act of wisdom.
The grass withers and the wood decays;
the flowers fade and the fruits fall—
such are the things of this kind.
That which is called the unconditioned of analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskṛta*) is so named.
The unconditioned of space (*ākāśa-asamskṛta*) is the locus of space; its essence is not a product of volitional action (*kṛtaka*), and it is therefore called the unconditioned of space.
The eighteen kinds of emptiness: internal emptiness,
external emptiness,
and internal-external emptiness.
Emptiness of emptiness,
great emptiness,
and the emptiness of the ultimate truth.
The emptiness of the conditioned,
the emptiness of the unconditioned,
and ultimate emptiness.
Emptiness of the beginningless,
emptiness of dispersion,
and emptiness of nature.
Emptiness of self-characteristics,
emptiness of all phenomena,
and emptiness of the unapprehendable.
The emptiness of non-existence;
the emptiness of existence;
the emptiness of both non-existence and existence.
These eighteen kinds of emptiness represent the sequence for dispelling delusion.
The delusions of sentient beings cannot be eliminated instantaneously.
Because hearing gives rise to attachment, contact produces speech, and these lead to stagnation,
it is necessary to employ eighteen kinds of emptiness to dispel delusions.
The *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explain their meaning in detail.
The meanings are vast and numerous;
they cannot be recorded in full.
There are three turnings: the first is the turning that reveals characteristics.
Second is the transformation through encouragement;
third is the transformation through realization.
As for the transformation through demonstration:
This refers to the manifestation of the characteristics of the four truths—
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path— whether with effort or without effort;
this is called the "turning that reveals characteristics."
Regarding "exhorting one another to turn [the wheel of Dharma]," this refers to exhorting others to know and exhorting them to practice the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths.
As the Sūtra says:
Suffering should be known;
its origin should be abandoned;
its cessation should be realized.
"The Path should be cultivated"—
this is the turning of the aspect of exhortation.
As for the turning of the aspect of realization:
The Buddha said:
"Suffering I have already known;
its origin I have already abandoned."
"Cessation has been realized by me;
the path has been cultivated by me.
This is called the transformation of the aspect of realization.
The Sūtra says:
"Turning the Wheel of Dharma three times throughout the great trichiliocosm"—
this refers to this very meaning.
It may also transform the teachings of the three vehicles,
which is termed the "three turnings.
The seven kinds of excellence consist of excellence in the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching.
First, its meaning is true and real;
second, its phrasing is skillful; third, its words are elegant;
fourth, its tone is pure.
5. Pure and unadulterated;
6. Fully endowed with purity;
7. The characteristic of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
The Five Sciences: Inner Science, Logic,
and Grammar.
The science of medicine,
the science of arts and crafts,
and the inner science.
That which is taught by the Buddha is called the internal treatise (śāstra).
Through the science of logic (hetuvidyā), one is able to refute the arguments of others and to establish one's own doctrine.

That which is called the *hetu-śāstra* (treatise on logic) is the skillful exposition of all distinctions among sounds and verbal expressions. That which is called the *śabda-śāstra* (treatise on grammar) is the elucidation of all varieties of phonemes.
There are four types of those who are proficient in the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*).
First, those who demonstrate the knowledge that distinguishes the causes of illness;
second, those who demonstrate the causes of illness.
Third, it is able to manifest the removal of diseases that have already arisen.
Fourth, it manifests that diseases already removed shall not recur.
Its meritorious activity clearly demonstrates the accomplishment of various worldly undertakings.
The Bodhisattva seeks all five of these fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*).

Chapter Five: The Dharma-Gate of the Names and Meanings of the Noble Ones (*ārya*). Regarding the names and meanings of the Dharma-gate of the Noble Ones, Chapter Five: The Seven Types of Trainees (*śaikṣa*). [1] One who is heading toward the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*).
The fruit of stream-entry;
the stage of the candidate for once-returning;
and the fruit of once-returning.
The stage of the candidate for non-returning (anāgāmipratipannaka),
the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala),
and the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala).
These are the seven types of practitioners of the Hīnayāna.
Because they have practiced but have not yet reached the goal,
they are termed "those who are heading toward" (mukha).
When their cultivation has reached its culmination,
it is termed "fruit.
These are the seven types of persons.
Regarding the teachings of the Hīnayāna,
their fruits and practices are not yet fulfilled,
and their forward progress has not ceased.
Therefore, they are called "trainees" (śaikṣa).
Only the Arhat has fulfilled the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and possesses no further training toward progress.
Therefore, they are called "those beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
However, within the Mahāyāna teachings,
only the Buddha is "beyond training."
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya: the fruit of srotāpanna,
the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin,
and the fruit of anāgāmin.
The fruit of Arhatship.
"Srotāpanna" is a term from the Central Kingdom;
here it is translated as "one who practices the outflow-free (anāsrava)."
It is also called "flowing against the current" or "discharging a debt.
A noble one (ārya) who has attained the first fruit gains the realization of non-self.
Having eternally severed the outflows (*āsrava*) of the truths and exhausted all delusions,
it is called the cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Since there is now true, untainted understanding, [one attains liberation].
Because one is able to turn forever away from birth and death,
it is called "going against the current";
that is, going against the current of birth and death.
Because the power of their untainted (anāsrava) strength is sufficient to dispel the sufferings of the three miserable realms (tridurgati),
they are established as those who have "resolved the debts of the three miserable realms.
As for the Sakṛdāgāmin:
As for the fruition, the subtle afflictions of the path of cultivation are exhausted all at once; these three types of persons eliminate them together.
Regarding the afflictions of the path of cultivation in the desire realm, they are divided into nine grades.
The first six are coarse;
the latter three are subtle.
A Sakṛdāgāmin abandons the first six grades.
Immediately thereafter, the three subtle moments of existence abide within the "thinning" (bhava) of the three grades;
therefore, the stage of "abiding in thinning" is established.
Because he preserves those vocal sounds, he is called a Sakṛdāgāmin.
Anāgāmin is also a term from the Western [Indic] language;
here it is translated as "Non-returner."
It is also called "Emerging from the Mud.
Having severed the afflictions of the desire realm until they are exhausted,
one is reborn in the two higher realms.
Having departed once, they do not return;
hence they are called "Non-returners" (Anāgāmin).
The afflictions of the desire realm are like muddy mire.
Because they have attained permanent liberation, it is said that they have "emerged from the mire of desire.
Retaining the transliteration from the Western [Indic] language, they are called *anāgāmin*. As for *arhat*:
This is called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).
It is also named "Slayer of Thieves" or "Non-arising."
